source_text: Quoniam comperi nonnullos, qui se plurimum sapere suis persuasionibus credunt, insanire, bacchari, et velut quiddam promptum ex oraculo dicere: postquam esse in mundo christiana gens coepit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum; ipsos etiam coelites, derelictis curis solemnibus, quibus quondam solebant invisere res nostras, terrarum ab regionibus exterminatos: statui pro captu, ac mediocritate sermonis contraire invidiae, et calumniosas dissolvere criminationes, ne aut illi sibi videantur, popularia dum verba depromunt, magnum aliquid dicere; aut, si nos talibus continuerimus a litibus, obtinuisse se causam putent, victam sui vitio, non assertorum silentio destitutam. Neque enim negaverim validissimam esse accusationem istam, hostilibusque condignos odiis nos esse, si apud nos esse constiterit causas, per quas suis mundus aberravit ab legibus, exterminati sunt dii longe, examina tanta moerorum mortalium importata sunt saeculis. Inspiciamus igitur opinionis istius mentem, et hoc quod dicitur, quale sit: summotisque omnibus contentionum studiis, quibus obscurari et contegi contemplatio rerum solet, an sit istud quod dicitur verum, momentorum parium examinatione pendamus. Efficietur enim profecto rationum consequentium copulatu, ut non impii nos magis, sed illi ipsi reperiantur criminis istius rei, qui se numinum profitentur esse cultores, atque inveteratis religionibus deditos. Ac primum ab his illud familiari et placida oratione perquirimus: postquam esse nomen in terris christianae religionis occoepit, quidnam invisitatum, quid incognitum, quid contra leges principaliter institutas, aut sensit aut passa est rerum ipsa quae dicitur appellaturque natura? Numquid in contrarias qualitates prima illa elementa mutata sunt, ex quibus res omnes consensum est esse concretas? Numquid machinae hujus, et molis, qua universi tegimur, et continemur inclusi, parte est in aliqua relaxata, aut dissoluta constructio? Numquid vertigo haec mundi, primigenii motus moderaren excedens, aut tardius repere, aut praecipiti coepit volubilitate raptari? Numquid ab occiduis partibus attolere se astra, atque in ortus fieri signorum coepta est inclinatio? Numquid ipse siderum sol princeps, cujus omnia luce vestiuntur, atque animantur calore, exarsit, intepuit, atque in contrarios habitus moderaminis soliti temperamenta corrupit? Numquid luna desivit redintegrare se ipsam, atque in veteres formas novellarum semper restitutione traducere? Numquid frigora, numquid calores, numquid tepores medii inaequalium temporum confusionibus occiderunt? Numquid longos habere dies bruma, revocare tardissimas luces nox coepit aestatis? Numquid suas animas expiraverunt venti? emortiusque flaminibus neque coelum coactatur in nubila, nec madidata ex imbribus arva succedunt? Commendata semina tellus recusat accidere, aut frondescere arbores nolunt? sapor frugibus esculentis, et vitis liquoribus mutatus est? olearum ex bacculis cruor teter exprimitur, nec lumini subministratur extincto? Animalia terris sueta, atque in aquis degentia non suriunt, nec concipiunt? foetus non in uteris sumptos suis moribus, et sua lege custodiunt? Ipsi homines denique, quos per inhabitabiles oras terrae sparsit prima incipiensque navitas, non matrimonia copulant nuptiarum solennibus justis? non dulcissimas procreant liberorum stirpes, non negotia publica, non privata, et familiares res agunt? non, ut cuique libitum est, per diversas artium, disciplinarumque rationes ingenia dirigunt, et studiosae referunt navitatis usuras? Non regnant, non imperant, quibus sors rerum attributa est talium? non auctiores quotidie dignitatibus et potestatibus fiunt? judiciorum disceptationibus praesunt? leges interpretantur et jura? Nonne omnia caetera, quibus vita succingitur et continetur humana, suis omnes in gentibus patriorum celebrant institutionibus morum? Cum igitur haec ita sint, neque ulla irruperit novitas, quae tenorem perpetuum rerum dissociata continuatione diduxerit: quid est istud, quod dicitur invectam esse labem terris, postquam religio christiana intulit se mundo, et veritatis absconditae sacramenta patefecit? Sed pestilentias, inquiunt, et siccitates, bella, frugum inopiam, locustas, mures, et grandines, resque alias noxias, quibus negotia incursantur humana, dii nobis important injuriis vestris atque offensionibus exasperati. Si in rebus perspicuis, et nullam desiderantibus defensionem, non stoliditatis esset diutius immorari, ostenderem profecto, replicatis prioribus saeculis, mala ista, quae dicitis, non esse incognita, non repentina; nec postquam gens nostra felicitate donari hujus vocaminis meruit, irrupisse has labes, et infestari coepisse discriminum varietate mortalia. Si enim nos sumus in causa, et in nostri criminis meritum excogitatae sunt hae pestes, unde novit antiquitas miseriarum haec nomina? unde bellis significatum dedit? pestilentiam, grandines, qua potuit notione signare, aut inter suas voces, quibus oratio explicabatur, assumere? Nam si novella sunt haec mala, et ab recentibus ducunt offensionibus causas, qui potuit fieri ut eis rebus verba formaret, quas nec ipsa sciebat expertam se esse, neque ullis comperisset majorum in temporibus factitatas? Penuria, inquit, frugum, et angustiae frumentariae arctius nos habent. Antiqua enim et vetustissima saecula necessitatis istius aliquando fuerunt expertia? nonne ipsa nomina, quibus censentur haec mala, testificantur et clamant, nullum ab his umquam immunem abisse mortalium? Quod si ad credendum difficilis res esset, testimoniis agere possemus auctorum, quantae, quoties, et quae gentes famem senserint horridam, et aggerata interierint vastitate. Casus frequentissimi grandinis accidunt, atque adierunt cuncta. In litteris enim priscis comprehensum et compositum non videmus, etiam imbres saxeos totas saepe comminuisse regiones? Difficiles pluviae sata faciunt emori, et sterilitatem indicunt terris. Immunis enim antiquitas malis ab his fuit? cum etiam flumina cognoverimus ingentia limis inaruisse siccatis. Pestilentiae contagia urunt genus humanum. Annalium scripta percurrite linguarum, fol. 3, diversitatibus scripta, universas discetis gentes saepenumero desolatas, et viduatas suis esse cultoribus. A locustis, a muribus, genus omne acciditur atque arroditur frugum. Historias ite per vestras, et ab istis pestibus instruemini, quoties prior aetas affecta sit, et paupertatis ad miserias venerit. Terrarum validissimis motibus tremefactae nutant usque ad periculum civitates. Quid, hiatibus maximis interceptas urbes cum gentibus superiora tempora non viderunt, aut ab hujusmodi casibus fortunas habuere securas? Quando est humanum genus aquarum diluviis interemptum? non ante nos? Quando mundus incensus in favillas et cineres dissolutus est? non ante nos? Quando urbes amplissimae marinis coopertae sunt fluctibus? non ante nos? Quando cum feris bella, et praelia cum leonibus gesta sunt? non ante nos? Quando pernicies populis venenatis ab anguibus data est? non ante nos? Nam quod nobis objectare consuestis bellorum frequentium causas, vastationes urbium. Germanorum et Scythicas irruptiones, cum pace hoc vestra et cum bona venia dixerim: quale sit istud quod dicitur, calumniarum libidine non videtis.
pass_a_gloss: Since I have discovered that some, who believe themselves to be very wise in their own persuasions, are raving, being frenzied, and as if something ready from an oracle is being said: after the Christian people began to exist in the world, the world has perished, the human race has been affected by many evils; also the heavenly ones, having abandoned their solemn cares, by which they were accustomed to visit our affairs, have been exterminated from the regions of the earth: I have decided, according to my ability and the mediocrity of my speech, to oppose envy and to dissolve calumnious accusations, so that neither they may seem to themselves to be saying something important while they utter popular words, nor, if we were to restrain ourselves from such disputes, they may think they have won the case, which has been conquered by their own fault, not by the silence of those who assert it. For I will not deny that this accusation is very strong and that we are worthy of hostile hatreds if it is established that there are causes among us by which the world has strayed from its laws, the gods have been exterminated, and so many mortal misfortunes have been imported into the ages. Let us therefore examine the mind of this opinion and what is being said, and, having set aside all the zeal of contentions, by which the contemplation of things is accustomed to be obscured and covered, let us weigh whether what is being said is true by an examination of equal moments. For it will certainly be brought about by the conjunction of consequent reasons that not we, but they themselves, who profess to be cultivators of the gods and dedicated to ancient religions, will be found to be guilty of this crime. And first, we ask them this with a familiar and calm speech: what unseen, what unknown, what contrary to the laws principally instituted has the nature of things itself, which is called and named, sensed or suffered since the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth? Have the first elements, from which all things are agreed to be composed, been changed into contrary qualities? Has any part of the machine and mass of the universe, by which we are covered and contained, been relaxed or dissolved in its construction? Has the whirlwind of the world, exceeding the primordial motion, begun to creep more slowly or to be seized by a precipitous volatility? Has the inclination of the stars to rise from the western parts and to become signs in the east begun? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, by which all things are clothed with light and animated with heat, become inflamed, grown cold, and corrupted the temperaments of its usual moderation? Has the moon ceased to renew itself and to be led back into its old forms by the constant restitution of new things? Have the colds, the heats, the moderate temperatures of unequal times perished in confusion? Has the winter begun to have long days and to recall the latest lights of the night in summer? Have the winds expired their souls? And have the flames died, so that neither the heaven is forced into clouds nor the fields, moistened by rains, follow? Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds that have been entrusted to it, or do the trees not want to sprout? Has the taste of the edible fruits and the liquid of the vines been changed? Does the blood of the olives, expressed from their berries, produce a foul cruor, and is no light provided to the extinguished? Do the animals, accustomed to the earth and dwelling in the waters, not suckle, nor do they conceive? Do the fetuses not preserve their customs and laws in the wombs? Do men, finally, whom the first and beginning navigation has scattered over the uninhabitable shores of the earth, not contract marriages with the solemnities of just nuptials? Do they not beget the most sweet offspring, not conduct public and private business, and familial affairs? Do they not, as it pleases each one, direct their talents through various arts and disciplines, and do they not repay the usuries of their studies? Do they not reign, do they not command, to whom the fate of such things has been attributed? Are they not becoming more dignified and powerful every day? Do they not preside over the disputes of judgments, interpret laws, and rights? Do they not celebrate all the other institutions of customs, by which human life is sustained and contained, in all their native lands? Since these things are so, and no novelty has burst in, which has disrupted the perpetual course of things by a discontinuous continuation: what is this thing that is being said, that a stain has been brought upon the earth since the Christian religion has introduced itself into the world and has revealed the hidden sacraments of truth? But, they say, pestilences, droughts, wars, scarcity of fruits, locusts, mice, and hail, and other harmful things, by which human affairs are attacked, are brought upon us by the gods, who are exasperated by your injuries and offenses. If, in clear things and those not requiring any defense, it were not stupid to linger, I would certainly show, by repeating the previous centuries, that these evils, which you say, are not unknown, not sudden; nor have they burst in and begun to afflict mortal things with a variety of dangers since our people has been deemed worthy of the happiness of this name. For if we are the cause, and these plagues have been devised as a merit of our crime, whence does antiquity know the names of these miseries? Whence has it given a sign of wars, pestilences, and hail, by what notion could it have signified them, or taken them up among its words, by which speech was explained? For if these evils are new and derive their causes from recent offenses, who could have formed words for these things, which it itself did not know to have experienced, nor had it learned from its ancestors in times past? 'The scarcity of fruits and the narrowness of grain have us in a tighter grip', it is said. Have the ancient and most ancient centuries not at some time been experienced in this necessity? Do not the very names, by which these evils are reckoned, testify and proclaim that no mortal has ever been immune from them? And if it were a difficult thing to believe, we could act with the testimonies of authors, how many and how often nations have felt the harsh famine and have perished in vast desolation. The most frequent accidents of hail occur and have affected all things. Have we not seen in ancient writings that even rocky rains have often threatened entire regions? Difficult rains make the crops die and indicate sterility to the earth. Was antiquity immune from these evils? For we have also known that even great rivers have been dried up by the mud. The contagions of pestilences burn the human race. Run through the writings of the annals, written in various languages, and you will learn that all nations have often been desolated and bereft of their cultivators. The entire genus is affected and gnawed by locusts and mice. Go through your histories and be instructed by these plagues, how often the previous age has been affected and has come to poverty and miseries. The cities are shaken by the strongest movements of the earth and tremble up to the point of danger. What of the greatest chasms, which have intercepted cities with nations, have not the previous times seen them, or have they had their fortunes secure from such accidents? When has the human race been destroyed by the floods of waters? Not before us? When has the world been burned and dissolved into ashes and embers? Not before us? When have the greatest cities been covered by the waves of the sea? Not before us? When have wars been waged with wild beasts and battles fought with lions? Not before us? When has the destruction of peoples been given by poisonous snakes? Not before us? For what you are accustomed to object to us, the causes of frequent wars, the devastations of cities, the irruptions of the Germans and Scythians, I say with peace and with good will: what is this thing that is being said, you do not see, carried away by the lust of calumnies.

choices.why: The Latin word 'bacchari' means to be frenzied or to be in a state of madness, and in this context, it is used to describe the behavior of those who are opposed to the Christian religion.
The Latin word 'oraculo' refers to a person or thing that gives wise or authoritative advice, and in this context, it is used to describe the source of the accusations against the Christians.

The Latin phrase 'christiana gens' refers to the people who follow the Christian religion, and in this context, it is used to describe the group that is being accused of causing the problems in the world.
